reference_title: Standard Practice Manual for Flexible Pavements

sections.title: Purpose
sections.summary: Establishes that UFC 3-250-03 provides guidance for preparing drawings and specifications for road and airfield flexible pavements built with asphalt cement materials, and gives design engineers, laboratory personnel, and project managers information on mix design, materials, production, and placement of asphalt mixtures.
sections.body: This UFC provides guidance for the preparation of drawings and specifications for road and airfield flexible pavements using asphalt cement materials. The term "asphalt" is used herein instead of bitumen or bituminous (a generic term for both asphalt and tar materials) because asphalt is the material typically used in pavement construction. In the past, tar or coal tar was used only in instances where fuel resistance was required. Due to problems with emissions, tar is no longer used in flexible pavement construction except occasionally as a sealer. This UFC also provides useful information for design engineers, laboratory personnel, and project managers concerning mix design, materials, production, and placement of the various asphalt mixtures.
key_points: Provides guidance for drawings/specifications for road and airfield flexible pavements using asphalt cement materials.
Uses the term "asphalt" rather than bitumen/bituminous because asphalt is the material typically used in pavement construction.
Tar/coal tar is no longer used in flexible pavement construction (emissions concerns) except occasionally as a sealer.
Serves design engineers, laboratory personnel, and project managers with mix design, materials, production, and placement guidance.
sections.applicability: Applies to any DoD project preparing drawings or specifications for asphalt flexible pavements on roads or airfields.

sections.title: Scope
sections.summary: Defines the scope of UFC 3-250-03 as prescribing the materials, mix design procedures, and construction practices used for flexible (asphalt) pavements across DoD road and airfield projects.
sections.body: This UFC prescribes materials, mix design procedures, and construction practices for flexible pavements.
key_points: Covers materials selection for flexible pavements.
Covers mix design procedures.
Covers construction practices.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever materials, mix design, or construction-practice guidance is needed for a flexible pavement project.

key_points: All documents cited throughout this UFC are compiled in Appendix A.

sections.title: Units of Measure
sections.summary: Explains that the International System of Units (SI) is the primary measurement system in this UFC, but inch-pound (IP) values govern in some cases due to applicable codes, standards, or industry practice, with the governing IP value shown parenthetically after the SI value.
sections.body: The primary system of measurement used in this UFC is the International System of Units (SI). In some cases, inch-pound (IP) measurements are the governing critical values because of applicable codes, accepted standards, industry practices, or other considerations where the IP measurements govern. The IP value is shown in parentheses following a comparable SI value.
key_points: Primary units are SI (International System of Units).
Inch-pound (IP) values govern in some cases due to codes/standards/industry practice.
The governing IP value is shown in parentheses following the SI value.
sections.applicability: Applies when interpreting any dimensioned value presented in this UFC.

sections.title: Background
sections.summary: Explains why flexible (asphalt) pavements are used: they form a resilient, largely waterproof, load-distributing medium that protects the base course and subgrade, tolerate minor consolidation/deflection without loss of performance, allow stage construction with locally available materials, and can be overlaid to add structural strength as loads or traffic increase.
sections.body: Asphalt mixtures (hot-, cold-, and warm-mix asphalt and other asphalt surfaces) provide a resilient, relatively waterproof, load-distributing medium that protects the base course and underlying pavement structure from the harmful effects of water and abrasion from traffic. Asphalt pavements wear, weather, and deteriorate from aging; therefore, maintenance of these pavements extends pavement life. The flexibility of asphalt mixtures allows a pavement structure to adjust slightly to consolidation of underlying layers or deflection due to load without affecting pavement performance. Flexible pavements also allow stage construction and use a range of construction materials, often leading to substantial savings through the use of locally available materials. Additional pavement courses are placed on existing pavements to provide additional structural strength as total loads increase or as traffic intensity increases. Design and construct the economical pavement that satisfies the objective of long pavement life.
key_points: Asphalt mixtures form a resilient, largely waterproof, load-distributing medium protecting the base course/subgrade from water and traffic abrasion.
Asphalt pavements wear, weather, and age, so maintenance extends pavement life.
Flexibility lets the structure tolerate minor consolidation of underlying layers or load-induced deflection without harming performance.
Flexible pavements permit stage construction and a range of, often locally available, materials for cost savings.
Additional courses may be overlaid on existing pavements to add structural strength as loads or traffic intensity increase.
The design/construction objective is an economical pavement with long service life.
sections.applicability: Provides the rationale for why flexible (asphalt) pavement systems are used and designed the way they are.

sections.title: Safety Considerations
sections.summary: Covers DoD's traffic-safety objective for pavement surfaces: non-skid texture, adequate grade control to shed surface water and reduce hydroplaning risk, avoiding polish-prone or friable aggregates that reduce skid resistance or generate foreign object debris (FOD), and construction techniques that ensure good asphalt-aggregate bond and aggregate retention.
sections.body: Department of Defense's (DoD) objective is to construct pavements that provide traffic safety. A non-skid surface is essential, and grade control is required to provide rapid removal of surface water to minimize the potential for hydroplaning. All pavement surfaces normally exhibit a sufficiently coarse texture to provide skid resistance. Avoid aggregate types known to have a history of polishing because they are probably the greatest cause of low skid resistance, prevalent in surface treatments and seal coats. Avoid aggregates having friable particles, as these tend to break down and form foreign object debris (FOD). Construction techniques are important for surface treatments and seal coats to ensure good bond between the asphalt and aggregate, providing aggregate retention. Pavement surfacing such as sealers that do not include aggregate are not applied in areas of high-speed traffic.
key_points: DoD's objective is a pavement surface that provides traffic safety, with adequate skid resistance and rapid surface-water removal to minimize hydroplaning.
Avoid aggregate types with a history of polishing -- a leading cause of low skid resistance, especially in surface treatments and seal coats.
Avoid friable aggregates that break down into foreign object debris (FOD), a particular concern on airfields.
Good asphalt-aggregate bond and aggregate retention depend on proper construction technique for surface treatments and seal coats.
Aggregate-free sealers are not applied in high-speed traffic areas.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting aggregates or specifying construction techniques for surface treatments/seal coats where skid resistance, FOD, or aggregate retention are safety concerns.
